Question: What is the overview of what each Part of the Data Protection Act 2018 covers?
Answer: The Act makes provision about the processing of personal data. Most processing of personal data is subject to the UK GDPR. Part 2 supplements the UK GDPR; Part 3 makes provision about the processing of personal data by competent authorities for law enforcement purposes; Part 4 makes provision about the processing of personal data by the intelligence services (and certain processing carried out by competent authorities jointly with the intelligence services); Part 5 makes provision about the Information Commissioner; Part 6 makes provision about the enforcement of the data protection legislation; and Part 7 makes supplementary provision, including provision about the application of the Act to the Crown and to Parliament.

Question: What did Section 1 of the Data Protection Act 2018 state in the 2026-03-10 version?
Answer: In the 2026-03-10 version of the Data Protection Act 2018, Section 1 provided an overview of the Act, stating that it makes provision about the processing of personal data, that most processing of personal data is subject to the UK GDPR, and that Part 2 supplements the UK GDPR. It further explained that Part 3 makes provision about the processing of personal data by competent authorities for law enforcement purposes, Part 4 makes provision about the processing of personal data by the intelligence services (and certain processing carried out by competent authorities jointly with the intelligence services), Part 5 makes provision about the Information Commissioner, Part 6 makes provision about the enforcement of the data protection legislation, and Part 7 makes supplementary provision, including provision about the application of the Act to the Crown and to Parliament.

Question: Which point-in-time versions of the Data Protection Act 2018 are indexed?
What amendment was made to Schedule 21 paragraph 12 of the Data Protection Act 2018 between the 2026-01-29 and 2026-04-07 versions?
Answer: Schedule 21 paragraph 12 was renumbered as paragraph 12(1) and a new sub-paragraph (2) was inserted by Schedule 9 paragraph 25(9)(a) and (c) of the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 (c. 18), with effect from 5 February 2026 (commenced by S.I. 2026/82, reg. 2(z11)). The new paragraph 12(2) provides that, in its application to transfers treated as approved by virtue of paragraph 10, section 74B(7) (transfers approved by regulations: monitoring) has effect as if the reference to section 74AA(4)(b) were omitted.

Question: In which version of the Data Protection Act 2018 was Section 13A, defining the meaning of "relevant offence" for the purpose of the right to erasure and empowering the Secretary of State to amend the table in Article 17(5) of the UK GDPR by regulations, first introduced?
Answer: Section 13A (Meaning of "relevant offence" for purpose of right to erasure), which empowers the Secretary of State by regulations to amend the table in Article 17(5) of the UK GDPR (subject to the affirmative resolution procedure), first appears in the 2026-03-31 version of the Data Protection Act 2018.

Question: Under the Equality Act 2010, what must an authority subject to the public sector duty regarding socio-economic inequalities do when making decisions of a strategic nature about how to exercise its functions?
Answer: An authority to which the section applies must, when making decisions of a strategic nature about how to exercise its functions, have due regard to the desirability of exercising them in a way that is designed to reduce the inequalities of outcome which result from socio-economic disadvantage.

Question: What did Section 1 of the Equality Act 2010 require of public authorities in the 2026-04-01 version?
Answer: In the 2026-04-01 version of the Equality Act 2010, Section 1 imposed a public sector duty regarding socio-economic inequalities, requiring an authority to which the section applies to have due regard, when making decisions of a strategic nature about how to exercise its functions, to the desirability of exercising them in a way designed to reduce the inequalities of outcome which result from socio-economic disadvantage. In deciding how to fulfil this duty, the authority must take into account guidance issued in accordance with subsection (2A) — namely guidance issued by the Scottish Ministers for devolved Scottish functions, by the Welsh Ministers for devolved Welsh functions, and by a Minister of the Crown in any other case.

Question: Which point-in-time versions of the Equality Act 2010 are indexed?
What new section was inserted into the Equality Act 2010 between the 2026-01-27 and 2026-04-07 versions, and by which amending Act?
Answer: Section 78A ("Equality action plans") was inserted into the Equality Act 2010 on 6 April 2026 by sections 33(2) and 159(3) of the Employment Rights Act 2025 (c. 36), commenced via S.I. 2026/323, reg. 3(1)(7). The new section empowers regulations to require employers (with 250 or more employees, subject to specified exceptions for public authorities) to develop and publish an "equality action plan" showing the steps they are taking in relation to gender equality matters such as addressing the gender pay gap and supporting employees going through the menopause, and to publish prescribed information relating to the plan.

Question: In which version of the Equality Act 2010 was Section 78A on equality action plans, requiring employers to develop and publish plans showing steps taken in relation to gender equality, first introduced?
Answer: Section 78A on equality action plans, requiring employers to develop and publish plans showing the steps they are taking in relation to gender equality, first appears in the 2026-04-06 version of the Equality Act 2010.

Question: Under the Online Safety Act 2023, what is the definition of a "user-to-user service"?
Answer: A "user-to-user service" means an internet service by means of which content that is generated directly on the service by a user of the service, or uploaded to or shared on the service by a user of the service, may be encountered by another user, or other users, of the service. It does not matter if content is actually shared with another user or users as long as the service has a functionality that allows such sharing, and it does not matter what proportion of content on the service is of that kind.

Question: What did Section 1 of the Online Safety Act 2023 state in the 2026-01-08 version?
Answer: In the 2026-01-08 version of the Online Safety Act 2023, Section 1 set out that the Act provides a new regulatory framework with the general purpose of making the use of internet services regulated by the Act safer for individuals in the United Kingdom. To achieve this, the Act imposes duties requiring providers of regulated services to identify, mitigate and manage risks of harm (including risks particularly affecting individuals with a certain characteristic) from illegal content and activity and from content and activity that is harmful to children, and confers new functions and powers on the regulator, OFCOM. The duties seek to secure that regulated services are safe by design and are designed and operated so that a higher standard of protection is provided for children than for adults, users' rights to freedom of expression and privacy are protected, and transparency and accountability are provided in relation to those services.

Question: Which point-in-time versions of the Online Safety Act 2023 are indexed?
What change was recorded for Section 66 (Requirement to report CSEA content to the NCA) of the Online Safety Act 2023 in the version dated 2026-04-07 compared with the 2025-08-20 version?
Answer: The 2026-04-07 version records new commencement information for Section 66: subsections (1) and (2) were brought into force on 7 April 2026 by S.I. 2026/262, reg. 2(1)(a) (note I110), and subsections (7)–(10) were brought into force on 7 April 2026 for specified purposes by S.I. 2026/262, reg. 2(1)(b) and reg. 2(2) (note I111). The previous 'Valid from 07/04/2026' marker preceding section 66 was correspondingly removed.

Question: In which version of the Online Safety Act 2023 was the offence of encouraging or assisting serious self-harm under section 184 first added as a priority offence in Schedule 7?
Answer: The offence of encouraging or assisting serious self-harm under section 184 was first added as a priority offence in Schedule 7 (paragraph 2A) in the 2026-01-08 version of the Online Safety Act 2023.

Question: Under the Human Rights Act 1998, what must a court or tribunal do when determining a question that has arisen in connection with a Convention right?
Answer: A court or tribunal determining a question which has arisen in connection with a Convention right must take into account any judgment, decision, declaration or advisory opinion of the European Court of Human Rights; any opinion of the Commission given in a report adopted under Article 31 of the Convention; any decision of the Commission in connection with Article 26 or 27(2) of the Convention; or any decision of the Committee of Ministers taken under Article 46 of the Convention, whenever made or given, so far as, in the opinion of the court or tribunal, it is relevant to the proceedings in which that question has arisen.

Question: What did Section 1 of the Human Rights Act 1998 state about 'the Convention rights' in the 2021-06-30 version?
Answer: In the 2021-06-30 version of the Human Rights Act 1998, Section 1 defined 'the Convention rights' as the rights and fundamental freedoms set out in Articles 2 to 12 and 14 of the Convention, Articles 1 to 3 of the First Protocol, and Article 1 of the Thirteenth Protocol, as read with Articles 16 to 18 of the Convention. It also provided that those Articles have effect subject to any designated derogation or reservation (per sections 14 and 15), that the Articles are set out in Schedule 1, and that the Secretary of State may by order amend the Act to reflect the effect of a protocol that the UK has ratified or signed with a view to ratification, provided no such amendment comes into force before the protocol is in force in relation to the UK.

Question: Which point-in-time versions of the Human Rights Act 1998 are indexed?
What amendment was made to Section 2 of the Human Rights Act 1998 between the 2020-10-21 and 2026-04-06 versions?
Answer: A new modification note (C5) was added recording that Section 2 was excluded (with effect from 25.4.2024) by the Safety of Rwanda (Asylum and Immigration) Act 2024 (c. 8), ss. 2(5)(b), 3, 10(1) (with ss. 4, 10(2)).

Question: In which version of the Human Rights Act 1998 was the modification of section 6(3)(b) by section 142C of the Mental Health Act 1983 (as inserted by the Mental Health Act 2025) first introduced?
Answer: The modification of section 6(3)(b) of the Human Rights Act 1998 by section 142C of the Mental Health Act 1983, as inserted by the Mental Health Act 2025, first appears in the 2026-04-06 version of the Act.

Question: What is the stated purpose of the Mental Health Act 1983?
Answer: The Mental Health Act 1983 is an Act to consolidate the law relating to mentally disordered persons.

Question: What did Schedule 6 of the Mental Health Act 1983 provide regarding repeals to the Mental Health (Amendment) Act 1982 in the 2026-02-18 version?
Answer: In the 2026-02-18 version of the Mental Health Act 1983, Schedule 6 (Repeals) listed the Mental Health (Amendment) Act 1982 (1982 c. 51) and provided for the repeal of Sections 1 to 33, Sections 35 to 61, subsection (1) of section 63 together with the words from the beginning to 'Act and' in subsection (2), Section 64(1), (2), (3), (5) and (6), Section 66, Section 68(2) and (3), Section 69(2), (3) and (4), the words 'sections 35(1) and (2) and 64(6) above extend to Northern Ireland' in section 70(2), Schedule 1, parts of Schedule 3 (including paragraphs 1 to 26 in Part I, sub-paragraph (a) of paragraph 35, paragraphs 40, 42, 45 and 46, sub-paragraph (a) of paragraph 50, sub-paragraph (a) of paragraph 51, paragraphs 52 to 55, 57 and 58, and all of Part II), and paragraphs 2 to 15 of Schedule 5.

Question: Which point-in-time versions of the Mental Health Act 1983 are indexed?
What amendment was made to Section 42 of the Mental Health Act 1983 in the version dated 2026-04-06 compared to the 2026-01-01 version?
Answer: A new subsection (2A) was inserted into Section 42 by section 35(2) of the Mental Health Act 2025 (c. 33), effective 18 February 2026. The new subsection allows the Secretary of State to impose conditions amounting to a deprivation of a patient's liberty under subsection (2) where satisfied that those conditions are necessary for the protection of the public from serious harm.

Question: In which version of the Mental Health Act 1983 was the provision permitting conditions amounting to a deprivation of a patient's liberty to be imposed on a conditionally discharged restricted patient (where necessary for the protection of the public from serious harm) first introduced?
Answer: The provision allowing conditions amounting to a deprivation of a patient's liberty to be imposed under subsection (2) where the Secretary of State is satisfied they are necessary for the protection of the public from serious harm (subsection (2A)) first appears in the 2026-02-18 version of the Mental Health Act 1983.

Question: When a court determines a question regarding the upbringing of a child or the administration of a child's property, what must be the court's paramount consideration?
Answer: When a court determines any question with respect to the upbringing of a child, or the administration of a child's property or the application of any income arising from it, the child's welfare shall be the court's paramount consideration.

Question: What did Section 1 of the Children Act 1989 state about the welfare of the child in the 2025-09-01 version?
Answer: In the 2025-09-01 version of the Children Act 1989, Section 1 provided that when a court determines any question with respect to the upbringing of a child or the administration of a child's property or the application of any income arising from it, the child's welfare shall be the court's paramount consideration. It also required the court, in any proceedings concerning the upbringing of a child, to have regard to the general principle that any delay in determining the question is likely to prejudice the welfare of the child. Subsection (2A), as set out in the 2025-09-01 version, further provided that a court, in the circumstances mentioned in subsection (4)(a) or (7), is to presume, unless the contrary is shown, that involvement of each parent within subsection (6)(a) in the life of the child concerned will further the child's welfare.

Question: Which point-in-time versions of the Children Act 1989 are indexed?
What change was recorded in the F42 commentary note for Section 8(4)(k) of the Children Act 1989 between the 2025-03-11 and 2026-03-25 versions?
Answer: The F42 commentary note for Section 8(4)(k), inserted by ss. 52(1) and 90(6) of the Domestic Abuse Act 2021 (c. 17), was updated to extend the end of the specified period from 26.11.2025 to 24.11.2026 for the commencements made on 27.11.2024 (E.W. specified areas), 11.3.2025 and 28.4.2025 (specified areas); the 5.3.2025 commencement retained the 26.11.2025 end date.

Question: In which version of the Children Act 1989 were sub-paragraphs (3) and (4) of Schedule 2 paragraph 12D first inserted, alongside the omission of words from Schedule 2 paragraph 12D(2)?
Answer: Sub-paragraphs (3) and (4) of Schedule 2 paragraph 12D were first inserted, and words in Schedule 2 paragraph 12D(2) were first omitted, in the 2025-09-01 version of the Children Act 1989.

Question: Under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984, what is the extent of the repeal of the Criminal Evidence Act 1965?
Answer: The Criminal Evidence Act 1965 (1965 c. 20) is repealed in its entirety — the whole Act is repealed generally in consequence of Part VII of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984.

Question: What did the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 state in the 2026-03-25 version regarding the repeal of the Criminal Evidence Act 1965 in Part III of the schedule of enactments repealed generally in consequence of Part VII?
Answer: In the 2026-03-25 version of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984, Part III of the schedule listing enactments repealed generally in consequence of Part VII provided that the Criminal Evidence Act 1965 (1965 c. 20) was repealed in its entirety (the whole Act), and that consequential repeals were made to the Post Office Act 1969 (1969 c. 48), specifically removing the words 'the Criminal Evidence Act 1965 and' from section 93(4) and repealing paragraph 77 of Schedule 4.

Question: Which point-in-time versions of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 are indexed?
What modification was made to Sections 1 and 2 of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 in the version dated 2026-04-07 compared to the 2025-11-21 version?
Answer: A new modification entry (C14 for Section 1 and C18 for Section 2) was added recording that S. 1 and S. 2 were applied in part (with modifications) from 7.4.2026 by The Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 (Application to Enforcement Officers) Regulations 2026 (S.I. 2026/303), regs. 1(1), 3, 4(a)/(b), and Sch. paras. 1-10, 11.

Question: In which version of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 was the heading and wording of section 114B changed from referring to 'labour abuse prevention officers' to 'enforcement officers'?
Answer: The change of section 114B's terminology from 'labour abuse prevention officers' to 'enforcement officers' first appears in the 2026-01-06 version of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984.

Question: What is the duty of the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971?
Answer: It is the duty of the Advisory Council to keep under review the situation in the United Kingdom with respect to drugs which are being or appear likely to be misused and whose misuse is having or appears capable of having harmful effects sufficient to constitute a social problem, and to give advice to one or more of the Ministers on measures (whether or not involving alteration of the law) which ought to be taken for preventing such misuse or dealing with related social problems. In particular, this includes advising on measures for: (a) restricting the availability of such drugs or supervising the arrangements for their supply; (b) enabling persons affected by the misuse of such drugs to obtain proper advice, and securing the provision of proper facilities and services for treatment, rehabilitation and after-care; (c) promoting co-operation between the various professional and community services with a part to play in dealing with related social problems; (d) educating the public (and in particular the young) in the dangers of misusing such drugs, and giving publicity to those dangers; and (e) promoting research into, or otherwise obtaining information about, any matter relevant to preventing the misuse of such drugs or dealing with related social problems.

Question: What did Section 1 of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 state about the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs in the 2023-12-31 version?
Answer: In the 2023-12-31 version of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971, Section 1 established the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs, constituted in accordance with Schedule 1. The Council's duty was to keep under review the situation in the United Kingdom regarding drugs being misused or likely to be misused where such misuse had or could have harmful effects sufficient to constitute a social problem, and to advise Ministers on measures to prevent misuse. These measures included restricting the availability of such drugs or supervising their supply, enabling affected persons to obtain proper advice and securing treatment, rehabilitation and after-care facilities, promoting co-operation between professional and community services, educating the public (particularly the young) about the dangers of misuse, and promoting research. The Council was also required to consider any matter relating to drug dependence or misuse referred to them by Ministers, including communications from international bodies relating to the control of dangerous or harmful drugs.

Question: Which point-in-time versions of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 are indexed?
What amendment was made to Section 4(1)(b) of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 between the 2022-06-28 and 2025-01-15 versions?
Answer: Section 4(1)(b) was further excluded by new modifications inserted into S.I. 2001/3998 — specifically regs. 6(2A), 8(7A), 8(8)(c), and 9(7A) — as inserted (E.W.S) on 31.12.2023 by The Misuse of Drugs (England and Wales and Scotland) (Amendment) (No. 2) Regulations 2023 (S.I. 2023/1345), regs. 1(2), 4(b), 7(b), 7(c), and 8(b). These exclusions appear as new modification notes C10–C13 in the 2025-01-15 version.

Question: In which version of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 was Brorphine first added to the list of controlled drugs?
Answer: Brorphine was first added to the list of controlled drugs in the 2024-03-20 version of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971.

Question: Under the Theft Act 1968, what is the basic definition of theft?
Answer: A person is guilty of theft if he dishonestly appropriates property belonging to another with the intention of permanently depriving the other of it; and 'thief' and 'steal' shall be construed accordingly. It is immaterial whether the appropriation is made with a view to gain, or is made for the thief's own benefit.

Question: What did Section 1 of the Theft Act 1968 state in the 2012-11-05 version?
Answer: In the 2012-11-05 version of the Theft Act 1968, Section 1 set out the basic definition of theft, providing that a person is guilty of theft if he dishonestly appropriates property belonging to another with the intention of permanently depriving the other of it, and that 'thief' and 'steal' shall be construed accordingly. It further stated that it is immaterial whether the appropriation is made with a view to gain or for the thief's own benefit, and that the five following sections of the Act have effect as regards the interpretation and operation of Section 1.

Question: Which point-in-time versions of the Theft Act 1968 are indexed?
What amendment was made to Section 24A(9) of the Theft Act 1968 between the 2010-01-12 and 2013-05-28 versions regarding the definition of an electronic money issuer?
Answer: In Section 24A(9), paragraph (c) of the definition of "Account" was substituted (footnote F27) so that instead of referring to "an issuer of electronic money (as defined for the purposes of Part 2 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000)", it now refers to "a person falling within any of paragraphs (a) to (j) of the definition of 'electronic money issuer' in regulation 2(1) of the Electronic Money Regulations 2011."

Question: In which version of the Theft Act 1968 was the reference to an electronic money issuer in section 24A(9)(c) changed from referring to Part 2 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 to referring to regulation 2(1) of the Electronic Money Regulations 2011?
Answer: The redefinition of the electronic money issuer reference in section 24A(9)(c) — from 'an issuer of electronic money (as defined for the purposes of Part 2 of the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000)' to 'a person falling within any of paragraphs (a) to (j) of the definition of "electronic money issuer" in regulation 2(1) of the Electronic Money Regulations 2011' — first appears in the 2013-04-01 version of the Theft Act 1968.

Question: Under the Sale of Goods Act 1979, what happens to a contract for the sale of specific goods if the goods, without the seller's knowledge, have perished at the time the contract is made?
Answer: Where there is a contract for the sale of specific goods, and the goods without the knowledge of the seller have perished at the time when the contract is made, the contract is void.

Question: What did Section 7 of the Sale of Goods Act 1979 state in the 2007-10-01 version regarding goods perishing before sale but after agreement to sell?
Answer: In the 2007-10-01 version of the Sale of Goods Act 1979, Section 7 provided that where there is an agreement to sell specific goods and subsequently the goods, without any fault on the part of the seller or buyer, perish before the risk passes to the buyer, the agreement is avoided.

Question: Which point-in-time versions of the Sale of Goods Act 1979 are indexed?
What amendment was made to Section 1 of the Sale of Goods Act 1979 in the version dated 2015-10-01 compared to the 2002-03-31 version?
Answer: Section 1 was amended by the insertion of new subsections (5) and (6), added (with effect from 1.10.2015) by Schedule 1 paragraph 9 of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 (c. 15), s. 100(5), commenced via S.I. 2015/1630, art. 3(g). The new subsections provide that certain sections or subsections of the Sale of Goods Act 1979 do not apply to a contract to which Chapter 2 of Part 1 of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 applies, and that where this is the case it is indicated in the section concerned.

Question: In which version of the Sale of Goods Act 1979 was the provision first introduced stating that certain sections or subsections of the Act do not apply to a contract to which Chapter 2 of Part 1 of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 applies?
Answer: The provision stating that certain sections or subsections of the Sale of Goods Act 1979 do not apply to a contract to which Chapter 2 of Part 1 of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 applies (section 1(5) and (6)) first appears in the 2015-10-01 version of the Act.

Question: Under the Consumer Rights Act 2015, what is the definition of a "consumer"?
Answer: A "consumer" means an individual acting for purposes that are wholly or mainly outside that individual's trade, business, craft or profession. Where a trader claims that an individual was not acting for purposes wholly or mainly outside the individual's trade, business, craft or profession, the trader must prove it.

Question: What did Section 2 of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 say about the key definitions of 'trader' and 'consumer' in the 2025-12-27 version?
Answer: In the 2025-12-27 version of the Consumer Rights Act 2015, Section 2 defined a 'trader' as a person acting for purposes relating to that person's trade, business, craft or profession, whether acting personally or through another person acting in the trader's name or on the trader's behalf. A 'consumer' was defined as an individual acting for purposes that are wholly or mainly outside that individual's trade, business, craft or profession, and a trader claiming that an individual was not acting for such purposes had to prove it.

Question: Which point-in-time versions of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 are indexed?
What amendment was made to Section 93 of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 in the version dated 2026-04-06 compared to the 2025-01-01 version?
Answer: Section 93 was amended by the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (c. 13), ss. 216(2)(a) and 339(1), to insert a new subsection (2A) providing that the Competition and Markets Authority may also enforce the provisions of Chapter 5. Consequential words in s. 93(3) were substituted by s. 216(2)(b) of the same Act to refer to subsections (1), (2) and (2A). Both changes were brought into force on 6 April 2025 by S.I. 2025/272, reg. 2(1)(2).

Question: In which version of the Consumer Rights Act 2015 was the Competition and Markets Authority first given power to enforce the provisions of the Chapter under section 93?
Answer: The provision empowering the Competition and Markets Authority to enforce the provisions of the Chapter (section 93(2A)) first appears in the 2025-04-06 version of the Consumer Rights Act 2015.

Question: Under the Modern Slavery Act 2015, does a victim's consent preclude a determination that they are being held in slavery or servitude or required to perform forced or compulsory labour?
Answer: No. Under section 1(5) of the Modern Slavery Act 2015, the consent of a person (whether an adult or a child) to any of the acts alleged to constitute holding the person in slavery or servitude, or requiring the person to perform forced or compulsory labour, does not preclude a determination that the person is being held in slavery or servitude, or required to perform forced or compulsory labour.

Question: What did Section 1 of the Modern Slavery Act 2015 state in the 2023-12-20 version regarding the offence of slavery, servitude and forced or compulsory labour?
Answer: In the 2023-12-20 version of the Modern Slavery Act 2015, Section 1 provided that a person commits an offence if they hold another person in slavery or servitude (where they know or ought to know the other is so held), or if they require another person to perform forced or compulsory labour (where they know or ought to know the other is being so required). These references were to be construed in accordance with Article 4 of the Human Rights Convention, and in determining whether a person was held in slavery or servitude or required to perform forced or compulsory labour, regard could be had to all the circumstances, including the person's personal circumstances such as being a child, family relationships, or any mental or physical illness that may make them more vulnerable. The 2023-12-20 version also specified that the consent of a person, whether adult or child, did not preclude a determination that they were being held in slavery or servitude or required to perform forced or compulsory labour.

Question: Which point-in-time versions of the Modern Slavery Act 2015 are indexed?
What amendment was made to Section 5 of the Modern Slavery Act 2015 between the 2023-01-30 and 2026-04-07 versions regarding penalties on summary conviction?
Answer: In Section 5(1)(b) and 5(2)(b), the words 'a term not exceeding 12 months' were substituted with 'the general limit in a magistrates' court'. Section 5(4) was also updated so that, in relation to offences committed before 2 May 2022, references to 'the general limit in a magistrates' court' are to be read as references to 6 months. These textual amendments are recorded under footnotes F1, F2, F3 and F4, originating from the Criminal Justice Act 2003 (Commencement No. 33) and Sentencing Act 2020 (Commencement No. 2) Regulations 2022 (S.I. 2022/500), which took effect on 28 April 2022.

Question: In which version of the Modern Slavery Act 2015 was the substantive content of section 11A (Enforcement by Gangmasters and Labour Abuse Authority), which provided for the Secretary of State to make arrangements with the Gangmasters and Labour Abuse Authority for its officers to act for the purposes of Part 1, removed?
Answer: The substantive provisions of section 11A of the Modern Slavery Act 2015 — including subsection (1) on arrangements with the Gangmasters and Labour Abuse Authority and subsection (2) on PACE powers for labour abuse prevention officers — were removed in the 2026-04-07 version, leaving only the section heading with omitted text.

Question: Under the Bribery Act 2010, what conditions must a function or activity meet to be considered a 'relevant function or activity' for the purposes of the Act?
Answer: A function or activity is a relevant function or activity if it falls within one of the specified categories (any function of a public nature; any activity connected with a business; any activity performed in the course of a person's employment; or any activity performed by or on behalf of a body of persons, whether corporate or unincorporate) and meets one or more of conditions A to C: Condition A is that a person performing the function or activity is expected to perform it in good faith; Condition B is that a person performing it is expected to perform it impartially; and Condition C is that a person performing it is in a position of trust by virtue of performing it. A function or activity qualifies even if it has no connection with the United Kingdom and is performed in a country or territory outside the United Kingdom.

Question: What did Section 1 of the Bribery Act 2010 state about offences of bribing another person in the 2023-02-07 version?
Answer: In the 2023-02-07 version of the Bribery Act 2010, Section 1 set out that a person (P) is guilty of an offence under either of two cases. Case 1 applies where P offers, promises or gives a financial or other advantage to another person, intending the advantage either to induce a person to perform improperly a relevant function or activity, or to reward a person for the improper performance of such a function or activity. Case 2 applies where P offers, promises or gives a financial or other advantage to another person and P knows or believes that the acceptance of the advantage would itself constitute the improper performance of a relevant function or activity. In Case 1 it does not matter whether the recipient of the advantage is the same person as the one performing the function or activity, and in both cases it does not matter whether the advantage is offered, promised or given directly or through a third party.

Question: Which point-in-time versions of the Bribery Act 2010 are indexed?
What amendment was made to Section 11 of the Bribery Act 2010 between the 2020-12-01 and 2024-01-15 versions?
Answer: A new subsection (1A) was inserted into Section 11 by regulation 22(2) of The Judicial Review and Courts Act 2022 (Magistrates' Court Sentencing Powers) Regulations 2023 (S.I. 2023/149), taking effect on 7 February 2023 at 12.00 p.m. The inserted provision specifies that, in the application of section 11 in England and Wales, the reference in subsection (1)(a) to 12 months is to be read as a reference to the general limit in a magistrates' court (or to 6 months in relation to an offence committed before 2 May 2022). At the same time, section 11(4)(a) was omitted by regulation 22(3) of the same Regulations.

Question: In which version of the Bribery Act 2010 was the provision stating that, in the application of section 11 in England and Wales, the reference to 12 months is to be read as a reference to the general limit in a magistrates' court (or to 6 months for offences committed before 2 May 2022) first introduced?
Answer: The provision in section 11(1A) stating that, in the application of that section in England and Wales, the reference in subsection (1)(a) to 12 months is to be read as a reference to the general limit in a magistrates' court (or to 6 months in relation to an offence committed before 2 May 2022) first appears in the 2023-02-07 version of the Bribery Act 2010.

Question: Under the Climate Change Act 2008, what is the duty of the Secretary of State regarding the net UK carbon account for the year 2050 in relation to the 1990 baseline?
Answer: It is the duty of the Secretary of State to ensure that the net UK carbon account for the year 2050 is at least 100% lower than the 1990 baseline, where the 1990 baseline means the aggregate amount of net UK emissions of carbon dioxide for that year and net UK emissions of each of the other targeted greenhouse gases for the year that is the base year for that gas.

Question: What did Section 1 of the Climate Change Act 2008 state about the 2050 target in the 2022-04-28 version?
Answer: In the 2022-04-28 version of the Climate Change Act 2008, Section 1 imposed a duty on the Secretary of State to ensure that the net UK carbon account for the year 2050 is at least 100% lower than the 1990 baseline, where the 1990 baseline is defined as the aggregate of net UK emissions of carbon dioxide for 1990 and net UK emissions of each of the other targeted greenhouse gases for the base year for that gas.

Question: Which point-in-time versions of the Climate Change Act 2008 are indexed?
What amendment was made to Section 29(1)(b) of the Climate Change Act 2008 between the 2022-01-09 and 2023-12-26 versions?
Answer: In the definition of 'UK removals' in section 29(1)(b), the words 'land use, land-use change or forestry' were substituted with 'processes, mechanisms or' by section 160 of the Energy Act 2023 (c. 52), with effect from 26 December 2023. As a result, 'UK removals' now refers to removals of a greenhouse gas from the atmosphere due to processes, mechanisms or activities in the United Kingdom.

Question: In which version of the Climate Change Act 2008 was nitrogen trifluoride first added to the table of targeted greenhouse gases in section 25(1)?
Answer: Nitrogen trifluoride was first added to the table of targeted greenhouse gases in section 25(1) in the 2023-02-03 version of the Climate Change Act 2008.

Question: Under the Freedom of Information Act 2000, what is a person who makes a request for information to a public authority entitled to?
Answer: Any person making a request for information to a public authority is entitled to be informed in writing by the public authority whether it holds information of the description specified in the request, and if that is the case, to have that information communicated to him.

Question: What did Section 1 of the Freedom of Information Act 2000 state in the 2026-03-10 version regarding the general right of access to information held by public authorities?
Answer: In the 2026-03-10 version of the Freedom of Information Act 2000, Section 1 established that any person making a request for information to a public authority is entitled to be informed in writing whether it holds information of the description specified in the request, and if so, to have that information communicated to them. This right was subject to sections 2, 9, 12 and 14, and the authority was not obliged to comply if it reasonably required further information to identify and locate the requested information and had informed the applicant of that requirement. The 2026-03-10 version also referred to the duty under subsection (1)(a) as 'the duty to confirm or deny'.

Question: Which point-in-time versions of the Freedom of Information Act 2000 are indexed?
What modification was made to the Freedom of Information Act 2000 between the 2026-02-05 and 2026-04-07 versions?
Answer: A new modification entry (C10) was inserted recording that the Act was modified on 10.3.2026 by The Surrey (Structural Changes) Order 2026 (S.I. 2026/264), specifically by arts. 1(1), 28(2)(f) and 40(2)(f).

Question: In which version of the Freedom of Information Act 2000 was The Armed Forces Commissioner first added as a public authority listed in Schedule 1?
Answer: The Armed Forces Commissioner first appears as a listed public authority in the 2026-03-02 version of the Freedom of Information Act 2000, in Schedule 1.

Question: Under the Terrorism Act 2000, what types of action fall within the definition of terrorism as set out in section 1(2)?
Answer: Action falls within section 1(2) if it: (a) involves serious violence against a person; (b) involves serious damage to property; (c) endangers a person's life, other than that of the person committing the action; (d) creates a serious risk to the health or safety of the public or a section of the public; or (e) is designed seriously to interfere with or seriously to disrupt an electronic system.

Question: How did Section 1 of the Terrorism Act 2000 define 'terrorism' in the 2025-07-05 version?
Answer: In the 2025-07-05 version of the Terrorism Act 2000, Section 1 defined 'terrorism' as the use or threat of action where: (a) the action falls within subsection (2); (b) the use or threat is designed to influence the government or an international governmental organisation, or to intimidate the public or a section of the public; and (c) the use or threat is made for the purpose of advancing a political, religious, racial or ideological cause. Subsection (2) specifies that qualifying action includes serious violence against a person, serious damage to property, endangering a person's life (other than the perpetrator's), creating a serious risk to public health or safety, or being designed seriously to interfere with or disrupt an electronic system. Under subsection (3), the use or threat of such action involving firearms or explosives is terrorism whether or not subsection (1)(b) is satisfied.

Question: Which point-in-time versions of the Terrorism Act 2000 are indexed?
What organisations were added to Schedule 2 of the Terrorism Act 2000 between the 2024-04-26 and 2026-02-23 versions?
Answer: Schedule 2 of the Terrorism Act 2000 was amended to add three new proscribed organisations under footnote F258: Palestine Action, Maniacs Murder Cult (MMC) (MKU) (MKY), and Russian Imperial Movement (RIM) (RID), including Russian Imperial Legion (RIL).

Question: In which version of the Terrorism Act 2000 were Palestine Action, Maniacs Murder Cult, and the Russian Imperial Movement first added to the list of proscribed organisations in Schedule 2?
Answer: Palestine Action, Maniacs Murder Cult (MMC), and the Russian Imperial Movement (RIM) were first added to the list of proscribed organisations in Schedule 2 of the Terrorism Act 2000 in the 2025-07-05 version.

Question: According to the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, what are the two types of unlawful conduct for which Part 1 provides offences and penalties?
Answer: Part 1 provides offences and penalties in relation to the unlawful interception of communications and the unlawful obtaining of communications data.

Question: What did Section 1 of the Investigatory Powers Act 2016 state in the 2025-11-17 version regarding the overview of the Act?
Answer: In the 2025-11-17 version of the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, Section 1 set out an overview of the Act, stating that it sets out the extent to which certain investigatory powers may be used to interfere with privacy. It provided that Part 1 imposes duties in relation to privacy and contains other protections, including offences and penalties for the unlawful interception of communications and the unlawful obtaining of communications data. It also noted that the regimes in Parts 2 to 7B cover interception of communications, obtaining of communications data, retention of communications data, equipment interference warrants, and bulk personal dataset warrants and authorisations, while Part 8 deals with oversight arrangements and Part 9 contains miscellaneous and general provisions including amendments to sections 3 and 5 of the Intelligence Services Act 1994.

Question: Which point-in-time versions of the Investigatory Powers Act 2016 are indexed?
What change was made to the definition of "the relevant period" in Section 24 of the Investigatory Powers Act 2016 between the 2025-07-08 and 2026-04-07 versions?
Answer: In Section 24, the definition of "the relevant period" was amended by removing the alternative wording marked by footnote F34 (which had offered both "third" and "ninth" working day options) and substituting it with a single fixed definition: the period ending with the third working day after the day on which the warrant was issued.

Question: In which version of the Investigatory Powers Act 2016 was the Department for Business and Trade, so far as relating to the Fair Work Agency, first added to the table of relevant public authorities in Schedule 4?
Answer: The Department for Business and Trade, so far as relating to the Fair Work Agency, was first added to the table of relevant public authorities in the 2026-04-07 version of the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, with designation under section 60A(7)(b) at Grade 7.

Question: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, what are the conditions under which a person is considered unable to make a decision for themselves?
Answer: A person is unable to make a decision for himself if he is unable to understand the information relevant to the decision, to retain that information, to use or weigh that information as part of the process of making the decision, or to communicate his decision (whether by talking, using sign language or any other means).

Question: What did Section 1 of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 state in the 2021-09-01 version?
Answer: In the 2021-09-01 version of the Mental Capacity Act 2005, Section 1 set out the principles applying for the purposes of the Act: a person must be assumed to have capacity unless it is established that he lacks capacity; a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision unless all practicable steps to help him do so have been taken without success; a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision merely because he makes an unwise decision; any act done or decision made under the Act for or on behalf of a person who lacks capacity must be done in his best interests; and before the act is done or decision made, regard must be had to whether the purpose can be as effectively achieved in a way that is less restrictive of the person's rights and freedom of action.

Question: Which point-in-time versions of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 are indexed?
What amendment was made to Section 44(3)(a) of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 between the 2020-11-02 and 2023-02-07 versions?
Answer: Section 44(3)(a) was amended on 7 February 2023 at 12.00 p.m. by The Judicial Review and Courts Act 2022 (Magistrates' Court Sentencing Powers) Regulations 2023 (S.I. 2023/149), regs. 1(2), 2(1), Sch. Pt. 1 table. The words specifying a maximum term of imprisonment 'not exceeding 12 months' on summary conviction were substituted with 'the general limit in a magistrates' court'.

Question: In which version of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 was the definition of "integrated care board" first added to Schedule AA1?
Answer: The definition of "integrated care board" as a body established under section 14Z25 of the National Health Service Act 2006 was first added to Schedule AA1 of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 in the 2022-07-01 version, replacing the previous definition of "clinical commissioning group".

Question: Under the Health and Social Care Act 2012, what outcomes are particularly relevant when the Secretary of State discharges the duty to secure continuous improvement in the quality of health services?
Answer: The outcomes relevant for these purposes include, in particular, outcomes which show: (a) the effectiveness of the services, (b) the safety of the services, and (c) the quality of the experience undergone by patients.

Question: What did Section 1 of the Health and Social Care Act 2012 provide regarding the Secretary of State's duty to promote a comprehensive health service in the 2025-06-19 version?
Answer: In the 2025-06-19 version of the Health and Social Care Act 2012, Section 1 substituted section 1 of the National Health Service Act 2006 to require that the Secretary of State must continue the promotion in England of a comprehensive health service designed to secure improvement in the physical and mental health of the people of England and in the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of physical and mental illness. It further provided that the Secretary of State must exercise the functions conferred by the Act so as to secure that services are provided in accordance with it, retains ministerial responsibility to Parliament for the provision of the health service in England, and that services provided as part of the health service in England must be free of charge except where charges are expressly provided for by or under any enactment.

Question: Which point-in-time versions of the Health and Social Care Act 2012 are indexed?

What update was made to the modification note regarding the power to amend the Health and Social Care Act 2012 conferred by the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 between the 2024-05-24 and 2026-02-05 versions?
Answer: The modification note (C1) was updated to record that the power to amend the Act conferred by sections 138(2)-(7) and 339(2)(c) of the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (c. 13), originally in force from 24.5.2024 for specified purposes, came fully into force on 1.1.2025 in so far as not already in force, by virtue of S.I. 2024/1226, regs. 1(2), 2(1)(2) (with Sch. paras. 10 and 20).

Question: In which version of the Health and Social Care Act 2012 was the requirement that an information standard must specify to whom it applies first introduced into Section 250?
Answer: The requirement that an information standard must specify to whom it applies (new subsection (2A), together with subsection (2B) listing the persons to whom it may apply) first appears in the 2025-07-07 version of the Health and Social Care Act 2012, in Section 250.

Question: Under the Pensions Act 2014, what are the conditions for a person to be entitled to a state pension payable at the full rate?
Answer: A person is entitled to a state pension payable at the full rate if the person has reached pensionable age and has 35 or more qualifying years.

Question: What did Section 2 of the Pensions Act 2014 state about entitlement to a state pension at the full or reduced rate in the 2024-04-08 version?
Answer: In the 2024-04-08 version of the Pensions Act 2014, Section 2 provided that a person is entitled to a state pension at the full rate if they have reached pensionable age and have 35 or more qualifying years, and at the reduced rate if they have reached pensionable age and have at least the minimum number of qualifying years but fewer than 35. The minimum number of qualifying years for the reduced rate was to be specified in regulations and could not be more than 10.

Question: Which point-in-time versions of the Pensions Act 2014 are indexed?
What modification to the Pensions Act 2014 is recorded in the 2026-04-06 version (compared with the 2023-12-31 version) by The Social Security (Gibraltar) Order 2024?
Answer: The 2026-04-06 version adds a new modification entry (C3) noting that the Pensions Act 2014 was modified by article 2 of The Social Security (Gibraltar) Order 2024 (S.I. 2024/149), coming into force in accordance with article 1(3) of that amending S.I. A parallel Scotland-specific modification (C2) was also added by article 2 of The Social Security (Gibraltar) (Iceland) (Liechtenstein) (Norway) (Further provision in respect of Scotland) Order 2024 (S.S.I. 2024/62).

Question: In which version of the Pensions Act 2014 was the modification note first introduced indicating that the Act is modified (in its application to Scotland) by The Social Security (Gibraltar) (Iceland) (Liechtenstein) (Norway) (Further provision in respect of Scotland) Order 2024 (S.S.I. 2024/62)?
Answer: The modification note recording that the Pensions Act 2014 is modified (S.) by The Social Security (Gibraltar) (Iceland) (Liechtenstein) (Norway) (Further provision in respect of Scotland) Order 2024 (S.S.I. 2024/62), art. 2, first appears in the 2024-02-21 version of the Act (added together with a parallel C3 entry referencing The Social Security (Gibraltar) Order 2024 (S.I. 2024/149)).

Question: Under the National Health Service Act 2006, must services provided as part of the health service in England be free of charge?
Answer: Yes. The services provided as part of the health service in England must be free of charge except in so far as the making and recovery of charges is expressly provided for by or under any enactment, whenever passed.

Question: What did Section 1 of the National Health Service Act 2006 state in the 2024-01-31 version?
Answer: In the 2024-01-31 version of the National Health Service Act 2006, Section 1 set out the Secretary of State's duty to promote a comprehensive health service. It required the Secretary of State to continue the promotion in England of a comprehensive health service designed to secure improvement in the physical and mental health of the people of England and in the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of physical and mental illness. For that purpose, the Secretary of State had to exercise the functions conferred by the Act so as to secure that services are provided in accordance with it, and retained ministerial responsibility to Parliament for the provision of the health service in England. The services provided as part of the health service in England had to be free of charge except in so far as the making and recovery of charges is expressly provided for by or under any enactment, whenever passed.

Question: Which point-in-time versions of the National Health Service Act 2006 are indexed?
What new modification was added to Section 2B(1) of the National Health Service Act 2006 in the 2025-09-01 version compared to the 2023-12-26 version?
Answer: A new modification entry (C7) was added to Section 2B(1) noting that the functions were made exercisable concurrently from 28.2.2024 by The East Midlands Combined County Authority Regulations 2024 (S.I. 2024/232), regs. 1(2), 22.

Question: In which version of the National Health Service Act 2006 was section 68A on the reconfiguration of NHS services first introduced?
Answer: Section 68A on the reconfiguration of NHS services, providing that Schedule 10A confers intervention powers on the Secretary of State in relation to the reconfiguration of NHS services, first appears in the 2024-01-31 version of the National Health Service Act 2006.

Question: What is the purpose of Chapter 1 of Part 1 of the Education Act 2002?
Answer: The purpose of Chapter 1 is to facilitate the implementation by qualifying bodies of innovative projects that may, in the opinion of the Secretary of State, contribute to the raising of educational standards in England, or, in the opinion of the National Assembly for Wales, contribute to the raising of educational standards in Wales.

Question: What did Section 1 of the Education Act 2002 state about the purpose and interpretation of Chapter 1 in the 2025-04-01 version?
Answer: In the 2025-04-01 version of the Education Act 2002, Section 1 set out the purpose and interpretation of Chapter 1, stating that the Chapter's purpose is to facilitate the implementation by qualifying bodies of innovative projects that may, in the opinion of the Secretary of State, contribute to raising educational standards in England, or, in the opinion of the National Assembly for Wales, contribute to raising educational standards in Wales. In forming such an opinion, the Secretary of State or the National Assembly for Wales must have regard to the need for the curriculum of any affected school in England to be balanced and broadly based and to promote spiritual, moral, cultural, mental and physical development, and for maintained schools in Wales must have regard to enabling pupils to develop in line with the four purposes set out in section 2(1) of the Curriculum and Assessment (Wales) Act 2021, providing appropriate progression, and being suitable for differing ages, abilities and aptitudes. The section also defined key terms including "the Chief Inspector," "children" (persons under nineteen), "education legislation," "maintained school," "qualifying body," "qualifying foundation," and "subordinate legislation."

Question: Which point-in-time versions of the Education Act 2002 are indexed?
What amendment to Section 1(2) of the Education Act 2002 is reflected in the version dated 2026-04-01 compared to the 2024-08-01 version?
Answer: In the 2026-04-01 version, the footnotes for Section 1(2) (notes F4, F5, and F6) were updated to extend the commencement of amendments made by The Curriculum and Assessment (Wales) Act 2021 (Consequential Amendments) (Primary Legislation) Regulations 2022 (S.I. 2022/744), Sch. 2 para. 6(2)(a), (b), and (c). The commencement dates were expanded from '1.9.2022 for specified purposes, 1.9.2023 for specified purposes' to also include '1.9.2024 for specified purposes, 1.9.2025 for specified purposes', covering the insertion of words in s. 1(2)(a), the omission of a word in s. 1(2), and the insertion of s. 1(2)(aa)(ab).

Question: In which version of the Education Act 2002 was the text of section 178 (training and education provided in the workplace for 14 to 16 year olds), including the amendments to section 83 of the Learning and Skills Act 2000, removed?
Answer: The substantive provisions of section 178 of the Education Act 2002 — including subsection (4) which amended section 83 of the Learning and Skills Act 2000 by substituting '15' for '16' and inserting a new subsection (11) — were removed in the 2026-04-01 version.

Question: Under the Housing Act 2004, what is the meaning of 'hazard' in relation to residential premises?
Answer: A 'hazard' means any risk of harm to the health or safety of an actual or potential occupier of a dwelling or HMO which arises from a deficiency in the dwelling or HMO or in any building or land in the vicinity, whether the deficiency arises as a result of the construction of any building, an absence of maintenance or repair, or otherwise.

Question: What did Section 1 of the Housing Act 2004 state in the 2022-10-01 version regarding the new system for assessing housing conditions?
Answer: In the 2022-10-01 version of the Housing Act 2004, Section 1 established that Part 1 provides for a new system of assessing the condition of residential premises and for that system to be used in the enforcement of housing standards. The new system operates by reference to the existence of category 1 or category 2 hazards on residential premises (see section 2) and replaces the existing system based on the test of fitness for human habitation contained in section 604 of the Housing Act 1985. The kinds of enforcement action involving the new system include improvement notices, prohibition orders and hazard awareness notices (Chapter 2); emergency remedial action and emergency prohibition orders (Chapter 3); and demolition orders and slum clearance declarations (Chapter 4). Section 1(4) defines 'residential premises' as a dwelling, an HMO, unoccupied HMO accommodation, or any common parts of a building containing one or more flats.

Question: Which point-in-time versions of the Housing Act 2004 are indexed?
What amendment was made to the Housing Act 2004 between the 2020-12-01 and 2025-12-27 versions regarding additional standards for housing in England?
Answer: Sections 2A and 2B and a cross-heading 'Additional standards for certain housing in England' were inserted into the Housing Act 2004 by sections 100(5) and 145(1)(7) of the Renters' Rights Act 2025 (c. 26), with effect from 27.12.2025 for the insertion of section 2B for specified purposes (otherwise prospective), as commenced by S.I. 2025/1354, reg. 2(a)(iii). Section 2A gives the Secretary of State power to set requirements for qualifying residential premises (covering matters such as state of repair, safety provisions and temperature), distinguishing 'type 1 requirements' enforceable under section 5 and 'type 2 requirements' enforceable under section 7, while section 2B defines 'qualifying residential premises' for the purposes of this Part.

Question: In which version of the Housing Act 2004 was the new section 2A, granting the Secretary of State power to set standards for qualifying residential premises in England, first introduced?
Answer: Section 2A, which empowers the Secretary of State to make regulations specifying requirements to be met by qualifying residential premises (covering matters such as state of repair, provisions for safety and comfort, and means of keeping premises at a suitable temperature), first appears in the 2025-12-27 version of the Housing Act 2004.

Question: Under the Immigration Act 2014's substituted section 10 of the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999, what are the three conditions that must be met before a family member of a person liable to removal may also be removed from the United Kingdom?
Answer: The first condition is that the family member is P's partner; P's child, or a child living in the same household as P in circumstances where P has care of the child; in a case where P is a child, P's parent; or an adult dependent relative of P. The second condition is that, where the family member has leave to enter or remain, that leave was granted on the basis of his or her family life with P; or, where the family member does not have such leave, in the opinion of the Secretary of State or immigration officer the family member would not be granted leave in his or her own right but would be granted leave on the basis of family life with P if P had leave to enter or remain. The third condition is that the family member is neither a British citizen, nor entitled to enter or remain in the United Kingdom by virtue of an enforceable EU right or of any provision made under section 2(2) of the European Communities Act 1972.

Question: What did Section 1 of the Immigration Act 2014 provide regarding the removal of persons unlawfully in the United Kingdom in the 2025-06-19 version?
Answer: In the 2025-06-19 version of the Immigration Act 2014, Section 1 substituted section 10 of the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999 to provide that a person may be removed from the United Kingdom under the authority of the Secretary of State or an immigration officer if they require leave to enter or remain but do not have it. It also allowed family members of such a person to be removed, provided three conditions were met: the family member was P's partner, child (or a child in P's household where P has care), parent (where P is a child), or an adult dependent relative; their leave (if any) was granted on the basis of family life with P, or they would only be granted leave on that basis; and they were neither a British citizen nor entitled to enter or remain by virtue of an enforceable EU right or section 2(2) of the European Communities Act 1972. A notice given to a family member invalidated any prior leave, and removal directions could be given under paragraphs 8 to 10 of Schedule 2 to the 1971 Act.

Question: Which point-in-time versions of the Immigration Act 2014 are indexed?
What modification was made to the Immigration Act 2014 between the 2024-02-13 and 2026-02-04 versions regarding its application in relation to the Safety of Rwanda (Asylum and Immigration) Act 2024?
Answer: A new modification note (C3) was added recording that the Immigration Act 2014 was excluded (with effect from 25.4.2024) by the Safety of Rwanda (Asylum and Immigration) Act 2024 (c. 8), ss. 2(5)(a), 5, 10(1) (with ss. 4, 10(2)).

Question: In which version of the Immigration Act 2014 was the reference to a DVS-registered person first added to the landlord/agent document requirements in section 34(1)?
Answer: The reference to a DVS-registered person (or a DVS-registered person of a prescribed description) was first added to the landlord and agent document requirements in section 34(1)(a)-(c) in the 2025-06-19 version of the Immigration Act 2014.

Question: Under the Trade Marks Act 1994, what are the absolute grounds on which a trade mark shall not be registered?
Answer: The following shall not be registered: (a) signs which do not satisfy the requirements of section 1(1); (b) trade marks which are devoid of any distinctive character; (c) trade marks which consist exclusively of signs or indications which may serve, in trade, to designate the kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, value, geographical origin, the time of production of goods or of rendering of services, or other characteristics of goods or services; and (d) trade marks which consist exclusively of signs or indications which have become customary in the current language or in the bona fide and established practices of the trade. However, a trade mark shall not be refused registration by virtue of paragraph (b), (c) or (d) if, before the date of application for registration, it has in fact acquired a distinctive character as a result of the use made of it.

Question: What did Section 1 of the Trade Marks Act 1994 state in the 2023-12-31 version?
Answer: In the 2023-12-31 version of the Trade Marks Act 1994, Section 1 defined a 'trade mark' as any sign capable of (a) being represented in the register in a manner which enables the registrar, other competent authorities and the public to determine the clear and precise subject matter of the protection afforded to the proprietor, and (b) distinguishing goods or services of one undertaking from those of other undertakings. It noted that a trade mark may, in particular, consist of words (including personal names), designs, letters, numerals, colours, sounds or the shape of goods or their packaging, and that references to a trade mark include collective marks (section 49) and certification marks (section 50).

Question: Which point-in-time versions of the Trade Marks Act 1994 are indexed?
What amendment was made to Section 12(2) of the Trade Marks Act 1994 between the 2021-11-26 and 2025-07-10 versions?
Answer: Section 12(2) was substituted (with effect from 31.12.2023) by regulation 5(2) of the Intellectual Property (Exhaustion of Rights) (Amendment) Regulations 2023 (S.I. 2023/1287), as recorded in textual amendment note F79. The replacement provides that subsection (1) does not apply where (a) there exist legitimate reasons for the proprietor to oppose further dealings in the goods for the purpose of protecting the proprietor's property (in particular, where the condition of the goods has been changed or impaired after they have been put on the market), and (b) the opposition to those dealings interferes with the rights of any other person no more than is necessary to achieve that purpose.

Question: In which version of the Trade Marks Act 1994 was the limitation introduced requiring that a proprietor's opposition to further dealings in goods must not interfere with the rights of any other person more than is necessary to protect the proprietor's property?
Answer: The requirement that the proprietor's opposition to further dealings in goods must not interfere with the rights of any other person more than is necessary to protect the proprietor's property first appears in the 2023-12-31 version of the Trade Marks Act 1994, in section 12(2).

Question: What are the main purposes of the Communications Act 2003 as set out in its long title?
Answer: The Communications Act 2003 is an Act to confer functions on the Office of Communications; to make provision about the regulation of the provision of electronic communications networks and services and of the use of the electro-magnetic spectrum; to make provision about the regulation of broadcasting and of the provision of television and radio services; to make provision about mergers involving newspaper and other media enterprises and, in that connection, to amend the Enterprise Act 2002; and for connected purposes.

Question: According to the 2025-10-01 version of the Communications Act 2003, what is the stated purpose of the Act as set out in its long title?
Answer: In the 2025-10-01 version of the Communications Act 2003, the long title states that it is an Act to confer functions on the Office of Communications; to make provision about the regulation of the provision of electronic communications networks and services and of the use of the electro-magnetic spectrum; to make provision about the regulation of broadcasting and of the provision of television and radio services; to make provision about mergers involving newspaper and other media enterprises and, in that connection, to amend the Enterprise Act 2002; and for connected purposes.

Question: Which point-in-time versions of the Communications Act 2003 are indexed?
What amendment to Section 198A(3)(b) of the Communications Act 2003 came into force on 1 January 2026, as reflected in the version dated 2026-01-01?
Answer: In Section 198A(3)(b), the word 'objectives' was substituted with 'requirements' so that the provision now refers to contributing towards the fulfilment of the public service requirements (as defined in section 264A). This change was made by Schedule 2 paragraph 25 of the Media Act 2024 (c. 15), s. 55(3)(a), and was brought into force on 1 January 2026 by S.I. 2025/1049, reg. 3(u).

Question: In which version of the Communications Act 2003 was Part 4B (Video-Sharing Platform Services) removed from the Act?
Answer: Part 4B (Video-Sharing Platform Services) was removed in the 2025-07-25 version of the Communications Act 2003.

Question: What is the stated purpose of the Employment Rights Act 1996 as set out in its long title?
Answer: The Employment Rights Act 1996 is an Act to consolidate enactments relating to employment rights.

Question: What did the Employment Rights Act 1996 state about its purpose and enactment in the 2026-02-18 version?
Answer: In the 2026-02-18 version of the Employment Rights Act 1996 (1996 CHAPTER 18), the Act is described as an Act to consolidate enactments relating to employment rights, dated 22nd May 1996, enacted by the Queen's most Excellent Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, in Parliament assembled.

Question: Which point-in-time versions of the Employment Rights Act 1996 are indexed?
What modification was applied to Part 2 of the Employment Rights Act 1996 between the 2025-12-29 and 2026-04-06 versions?
Answer: In the 2026-04-06 version, a new modification entry C20 was added recording that Part 2 of the Employment Rights Act 1996 was applied (with modifications) on 6.4.2026 by the Employment Rights Act 2025 (c. 36), ss. 51(3) and 159(3), brought into force by S.I. 2026/323, reg. 3(1)(21).

Question: In which version of the Employment Rights Act 1996 was the heading of Part 2A expanded from 'Zero hours workers' to 'Zero hours workers and similar'?
Answer: The Part 2A heading was expanded to read 'Zero hours workers and similar' in the 2026-01-06 version of the Employment Rights Act 1996, with the words 'and similar' inserted into the Part 2A heading.

Question: Who are the directors that make up the court of directors of the Bank of England, as appointed by Her Majesty?
Answer: The court consists of the following directors appointed by Her Majesty: a Governor; a Deputy Governor for financial stability; a Deputy Governor for markets and banking; a Deputy Governor for monetary policy; a Deputy Governor for prudential regulation; and not more than 9 non-executive directors.

Question: What did Section 1 of the Bank of England Act 1998 state about the composition of the court of directors in the 2025-01-01 version?
Answer: In the 2025-01-01 version of the Bank of England Act 1998, Section 1 provided that there shall continue to be a court of directors of the Bank, consisting of directors appointed by Her Majesty: a Governor, a Deputy Governor for financial stability, a Deputy Governor for markets and banking, a Deputy Governor for monetary policy, a Deputy Governor for prudential regulation, and not more than 9 non-executive directors. Schedule 1 was to have effect with respect to the court.

Question: Which point-in-time versions of the Bank of England Act 1998 are indexed?
What amendment was made to Section 9U(3)(d) of the Bank of England Act 1998 in the 2025-11-30 version compared to the 2024-03-01 version?
Answer: Words in section 9U(3)(d) were substituted on 30 November 2025 by The Financial Services and Markets Act 2023 (Capital Buffers and Macro-prudential Measures) (Consequential Amendments) Regulations 2025 (S.I. 2025/1023), regulation 2, replacing the reference to the Capital Requirements (Capital Buffers and Macro-prudential Measures) Regulations 2014 with a reference to the Capital Buffers and Macro-prudential Measures Regulations 2025 (S.I. 2025/653).

Question: In which version of the Bank of England Act 1998 was the exclusion of Schedule 6A paragraph 17(9)(b) by the Insurance and Reinsurance Undertakings (Prudential Requirements) Regulations 2023 (S.I. 2023/1347) first added to the modifications?
Answer: The exclusion of Schedule 6A paragraph 17(9)(b) by the Insurance and Reinsurance Undertakings (Prudential Requirements) Regulations 2023 (S.I. 2023/1347), regs. 1(2), 3(2), with effect from 30.6.2024, first appears in the 2024-06-30 version of the Bank of England Act 1998.

Question: What matters must the holder of the office of Senior President of Tribunals have regard to when carrying out the functions of that office?
Answer: The Senior President of Tribunals must have regard to: (a) the need for tribunals to be accessible; (b) the need for proceedings before tribunals to be fair and to be handled quickly and efficiently; (c) the need for members of tribunals to be experts in the subject-matter of, or the law to be applied in, cases in which they decide matters; and (d) the need to develop innovative methods of resolving disputes that are of a type that may be brought before tribunals.

Question: What did Section 2 of the Serious Crime Act 2007 provide regarding the Senior President of Tribunals in the 2024-04-30 version?
Answer: In the 2024-04-30 version, Section 2 provided that Her Majesty may, on the recommendation of the Lord Chancellor, appoint a person to the office of Senior President of Tribunals, with Schedule 1 making further provision about the office and recommendations for appointment. The holder must, in carrying out the functions of the office, have regard to the need for tribunals to be accessible; for proceedings to be fair and handled quickly and efficiently; for tribunal members to be experts in the subject-matter or law applied; and to develop innovative methods of resolving disputes. "Tribunals" in this section means the First-tier Tribunal, the Upper Tribunal, employment tribunals, and the Employment Appeal Tribunal.

Question: Which point-in-time versions of the Serious Crime Act 2007 are indexed?
What amendment was made to Section 8(2) of the Serious Crime Act 2007 between the 2024-03-31 and 2026-03-18 versions?
Answer: Section 8(2) was amended by the insertion of new words referring to 'paragraph 2 of Schedule A1 to the Employment Tribunals Act 1996' (marked as F25). This insertion was made by Schedule 5 paragraph 28 of the Judicial Review and Courts Act 2022 (c. 35), via section 51(4), and was brought into force on 25 April 2024 by S.I. 2024/568, regulation 2(b)(viii). Additionally, a new modification (C3) was added applying section 8(3)-(5) by virtue of Schedule A1 paragraph 2(7) of the Employment Tribunals Act 1996, as inserted by Schedule 5 paragraph 1 of the Judicial Review and Courts Act 2022.

Question: In which version of the Serious Crime Act 2007 was the reference to paragraph 2 of Schedule A1 to the Employment Tribunals Act 1996 added to section 8(2)?
Answer: The reference to paragraph 2 of Schedule A1 to the Employment Tribunals Act 1996 was added to section 8(2) of the Serious Crime Act 2007 in the 2024-04-25 version.
